articles.title: Wall Street firms are linking bonuses to AI
articles.summary: New York: AI skills are starting to count toward pay and promotion on Wall Street, with nearly a quarter of financial firms tying raises, bonuses or promotions to employees' proficiency with the technology, a survey showed.Another 30 per cent require employees to disclose their use of artificial intelligence tools in formal performance reviews, according to the survey by Selby Jennings, a financial-services recruitment firm.The findings point to a broader shift on Wall Street as firms seek tangible returns from their investment in the technology."Companies are no longer just seeing if their employees are using AI tools but are also monitoring its impact on output and contribution to business results," Dylan Gomez, executive director at Selby Jennings, told Reuters."While currently there is no established formula on how much compensation is getting tied to AI usage and performance, we expect this to become more defined by next year," Gomez added.The survey found that 42% of respondents had introduced formal criteria to evaluate employees' AI skills, while 30 per cent had created dedicated teams or roles focused on tracking whether their AI investments were delivering results.The firm polled 500 executives across the finance industry.

articles.summary: Wholesale prices rose to 11.39% on-year in September, from 9.92% in August, official data released by the commerce and industry ministry on Wednesday showed, due to a sharp rise in fuel and power, food and manufactured product prices.A Reuters poll of economists had, earlier this month, estimated wholesale inflation at 10.18% for the month.Meanwhile, data from earlier this week showed that the country’s retail inflation rose to 5.54% in September 2026 from 4.83% in August, owing to a sharp rise in food prices, particularly vegetables.Also Read: India's retail inflation quickens to 5.54% in September from 4.83% in August, hits near two-year highInflation in fuel and power rose to 25.85% in September from 22.93% in August, while inflation in manufactured products increased to 9.76% from 8.37%.Inflation in primary articles, which include food articles, non-food articles and minerals, rose to 8.67% from 7.76% over the same period.The wholesale food index, which includes food articles and manufactured food products, recorded inflation of 8.66% in September, up from 7.05% in August.Among the key drivers of wholesale inflation were mineral oils, food articles, crude petroleum and natural gas, coal and lignite, basic metals, chemicals, textiles, rubber and plastic products, and electrical equipment, the ministry said.Also Read: Double trouble at the dinner table: When will food prices normalise for Indians?An ET Online survey of economists from earlier this month, showed that food inflation is likely to remain elevated over the coming months, with some expecting it to rise to 7-8% over the next three to six months. ICRA’s Aditi Nayar and ANZ’s Dhiraj Nim had flagged to ET Online that below-average reservoir levels are a concern for winter crops, with the impact on food prices depending on crop output and adverse weather conditions.Higher global commodity prices and energy costs add to the pressure on food prices.Elevated crude oil prices can raise farm, irrigation and transportation costs, while higher liquefied natural gas (LNG) prices can increase fertiliser costs. India’s dependence on imported edible oils also leaves the category exposed to global price movements, while higher freight, packaging and crop-protection costs could add to the cost of bringing food to market.In early October, the RBI hiked benchmark repo rate to 5.5% in first such increase since February 2023, with Governor Sanjay Malhotra flagging “it is clear that inflation and its outlook are not benign as they were last year.”The September WPI inflation data was released under the revised series, introduced in June with 2022-23 as the base year to better reflect the economy’s current structure. articles.title: AI skills redraw entry-level jobs map
articles.summary: India’s IT-BPM sector is set to revive fresher hiring after a sharp contraction, but the recovery is rewiring the skills companies seek in graduates.Fresher hiring in the sector is projected to rise to up to 2.1 lakh in FY27, after falling to an estimated 1.75 lakh in FY26 from 4 lakh in FY22, according to technology consulting and talent advisory firm HAN Digital’s IT-BPM Graduate Hiring Outlook 2027.However, demand is increasingly shifting towards artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), data engineering, cybersecurity and other specialised technology roles, away from conventional entry-level coding and business process outsourcing jobs.IT Services players will remain the largest employers of the sector’s freshers, accounting for about 60% of hires, though growth now will be concentrated in AI-adjacent and specialised roles.GCCs are the fastest-growing channel, expected to recruit 28% of talent as they expand intake into Tier II/III cities. Pure-play BPOs’ share keeps shrinking, mirroring the shift from routine execution to specialised, AI-adjacent work.“The rise in fresher hiring reflects a structural reset in how IT services firms are building their talent pyramid,” said Saravanan Balasundaram, CEO, HAN Digital Solution.As system integrators and IT Service providers sign more AI, data engineering and AI-enabled deals with existing and new clients, the bench capacity reduced by layoffs over the last few years can no longer absorb the demand, he said. “At the same time, new AI roles in data engineering, AI testing, annotation and model operations are opening up at the base of the pyramid, where AI-ready graduates can be skilled and deployed at scale, while mid-level hiring in the four+ years band remains under cost and productivity pressure.”The shift is changing expectations from new recruits. As AI tools take over parts of routine coding, testing and repetitive tasks, employers increasingly want graduates who can work with AI systems, validate their outputs and apply technology to business problems.The skillsets that companies are hiring for are definitely changing, said Sangeeta Gupta, senior VP, Nasscom. “It’s much more focused on AI capabilities – there are new jobs that are also opening up with data centres coming up.”The traditional model of bulk hiring, six months of training and deployment is also changing. “The new kind of freshers companies need are AI-native,” she said.This change is also visible in salaries. Freshers with AI-allied skills can command significantly higher pay, indicating that employers are increasingly paying for specialised skills rather than graduate headcount alone.India’s Tier-1 IT Services players’ 2027 fresher model offers Rs 12–22 lakh for select specialised engineers in AI, data engineering, cybersecurity and enterprise tech as the premium shifts toward specialised technology capability, found the report.“This would never happen in the past,” said Gupta, citing Infosys’ plan to offer up to Rs 21 lakh for certain specialised tech roles. Entry-level salaries across ITeS meanwhile have largely stagnated at Rs 3-4 lakh for years.Recruitment geography is widening too. Bengaluru remains the leading fresher destination, accounting for an estimated 25% of onboarding, followed by Delhi-NCR at 17%, Hyderabad at 16%, Chennai at 15% and Mumbai and Pune at 10% each. Yet, Tier 2/3 corridors are outpacing metro growth, albeit on a smaller base, at 35% year-on-year.Coimbatore, Jaipur, Kochi, Indore, Ahmedabad, and Visakhapatnam are attracting freshers via local GCC centres and IT services players seeking lower-cost talent pools beyond major metros.

We referred the matter to the FBI, and we're grateful to the agents and prosecutors who moved quickly to make an arrest. The FBI's investigation is ongoing and we will continue to support their work," an OpenAI spokesperson said.— OpenAINewsroom (@OpenAINewsroom) "At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data. The employee was terminated," the statement said.The complaint does not detail what Alfozan might have wanted to do with any captured communications, but the company said the device was sophisticated, designed to evade detection and featured advanced encryption and audio monitoring capabilities.OpenAI said it had evidence the employee planned to place other listening devices throughout other parts of the office building for the purpose of recording meetings."This alleged attempt by a Saudi national to steal sensitive communications from OpenAI was taken extremely seriously. Theft of intellectual property involving cutting-edge super intelligence technology poses a serious threat to our national security," Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a statement on X.Alfozan made his first court appearance Tuesday on a charge of using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications. It was not immediately clear if he had a lawyer who could speak on his behalf. He is due back in court on Oct 19.The recording device was found September 30 concealed in toilet paper and inserted into a USB port on the back of a television in an executive conference room, according to the complaint.Though the conference room where the recording device was found did not have a security camera at the time the object was installed, closed-circuit television footage inside the company's offices revealed that Alfozan was near the conference room on nearly a dozen occasions last month despite not having any authority to access the space or participate in meetings there, the complaint says.The company subsequently added a camera to the room that last week captured Alfozan entering and checking behind the television where the recording device had been installed, according to the FBI.Also read: OpenAI and Anthropic fear a major AI crisis in the next 6 to 12 months. articles.title: Flights to Saudi Arabia suspended until Oct 17
articles.summary: Mumbai: Airlines have suspended flights to Saudi Arabia until October 17 after the kingdom's aviation regulator suspended operations at Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport, disrupting travel across the region and leaving passengers seeking alternative routes.Air India, Air India Express and IndiGo have suspended services to Riyadh, Dammam and Jeddah, with IndiGo also suspending flights to Medina, according to an advisory issued by the Indian Embassy in Riyadh on Tuesday. Akasa Air has also suspended flights to Riyadh and Jeddah until the same date.The disruption has spread to international carriers. Emirates cancelled multiple services to Riyadh, Dammam, Jeddah and Medina on October 12 and 13, while Etihad Airways cancelled Abu Dhabi-Riyadh flights through October 19 and services to Jeddah and Dammam through October 14. Flydubai has reported cancellations affecting Riyadh, Dammam and Abha through October 19. Qatar Airways has suspended flights to Riyadh and Dammam without announcing a resumption date. Gulf Air has cancelled Riyadh services through October 17.European carriers have also extended disruptions. Lufthansa Group has cancelled Riyadh flights through October 16, while Air France-KLM has suspended services to the Saudi capital through the end of October. Philippine Airlines has extended its Riyadh suspension until November 29.The suspensions come after an attack at Riyadh airport on October 10 killed Indian national Mohammed Yousef Ali and injured 11 others. Four of the injured Indians remain in intensive care, four are receiving treatment in hospital wards and three have been discharged, the embassy said.While operations at Riyadh airport have been suspended, flights at other major Saudi airports, including Dammam, Jeddah and Medina, continue, though they face disruptions. Saudi carriers Saudia and Flynas are operating some scheduled services, according to the embassy.The disruption is forcing passengers to check alternative travel options as airlines adjust their schedules. Indian nationals needing to leave Saudi Arabia in an emergency can consider flights from neighbouring Gulf countries, particularly Qatar and Bahrain, subject to obtaining the required visas, the embassy said.It advised Indian nationals to remain in contact with their airlines to verify flight status. It also said Saudi authorities would allow visitors, tourists, Umrah pilgrims and business travellers who overstayed their visas because flights were unavailable to leave without paying fines.The Indian Embassy in Riyadh and the Consulate in Jeddah continue to operate normally. The embassy has opened a 24-hour control room to assist Indian nationals as the situation evolves.

articles.title: Blackstone readies $100 bn cheque for India
articles.summary: India is the best performing market for Blackstone, president and chief operating officer Jonathan Gray told Sruthijith KK in an interview. The world’s largest alternative asset manager aims to double its investment in India to $100 billion, he said, adding that the sentiment on the country is still positive. Edited excerpts:From your perch, what are two causes for concern about the global economy and two for optimism?Obviously the wars in Russia, Ukraine, as well as West Asia, which are causing commodity prices to go up. Agricultural prices are impacted, and that has pushed central banks… part of the reason they’ve had to move to raise rates as opposed to lowering. That ties to my second concern–the rising cost of capital. Interest rates around the world are going up. We’ve seen 10-year treasuries in the US go up by 80 bps in the third quarter. In Europe, we’ve seen a pretty significant rise, particularly in France. This is really a combination of the war, or the wars, and the inflation caused by that, as well as concerns around government deficits.Also Read: Blackstone has $100-billion plans for India in 5 years, says COO Jonathan GrayAdd to the mix this huge AI capex build and what that is doing in terms of demand for capital. All of that will likely lead to multiples coming down a bit for assets. That’s the major impact.On the positive side, I would say two things. One is we still see a lot of economic momentum. In the US, very strong revenue growth at our companies. In India, strong revenue growth. The second thing is AI diffusing into the economy, and the productivity we’re beginning to see at our companies, which is pretty remarkable.On the AI infrastructure build-out, is this investment sustainable? McKinsey’s State of the AI report earlier this year said adoption is deepening, but enterprise returns are flatlining. We’re also seeing some concern with AI debt…Whenever you have a large innovation and then capital flowing towards it, there’s a risk that things go out of kilter. First off, the demand is just continuing to grow, and I would say at our companies, the returns on investment seem remarkable. They’re finding new ways to use this technology. We have a garage door opening company that’s using AI visualisation tools to recognise when the package is coming from Amazon, then automatically opening the door. They’ve created a $50 million business that they think will be a $500 million business.We’re finding use cases in legal and accounting and all these different areas, and our teams at times can find it difficult to get this deployed, to get the technology right. If you think about a classic bubble–telecom infrastructure in the 90s–the supply was built with leverage well in advance of the demand. It turned out to be excessive, and ultimately there were a lot of losses.In this case, most of this is being built out by the biggest companies in the world who have very healthy balance sheets. What we’re seeing is demand is running ahead of supply, and the supply of compute is constrained by getting entitlements, getting a power plant, getting turbines, getting chips, amassing capital. We have a fundamental shortage of compute, and that is supporting the value. Most of this is now being contracted by very large companies such as Microsoft, Amazon, Google.How does the firm view the Indian economy in the medium and long term?Start with the short term. Obviously, there’s been some negativity because the wars have driven up energy costs. There’s been some pressure on IT services valuations with concerns about AI disruption and the market was trading at a very high multiple here. We’ve seen the sentiment in India, people have gotten overly negative, (but) when you look at the medium and longer term, you’ve got an economy that’s growing at 7%-plus, a very young population.There’s a lot of things that give India an edge over time, and I see it as the fastestgrowing major economy for many decades to come. As an investor with a long-term perspective, we say this is actually a pretty good moment. As the market’s pulled back, that creates a better entry point for us. We take a long-term view. I remember back after the financial crisis, most investors were saying, “Oh, India, gosh, I don’t wanna do that.” We stuck through it. That turned out to be the right decision. This is nothing like that. But again, if you look at the long-term fundamentals of this economy–the rising middle class, the opportunities that will create, India’s opportunity to be more of a manufacturing powerhouse globally–there are a lot of interesting places to deploy capital.You mentioned IT services and pressure on the sector. How do you see that playing out?I think these IT services companies are much more adaptable than people realise. They’ve moved from just providing services to be AI deployment companies. If you think about most enterprises, it’s not like I could hand you Claude code or Codex and say, “Change your business. Make your company different.”You need a partner to come in and say, “This is how you’re going to change your workflow. This is how you’re going to do your financial reporting.” India, given its strength in IT services, is a natural to help bridge this world. I also think there’s a big opportunity in India in the infrastructure we were talking about earlier. We’ve got AirTrunk here to do hopefully sizeable things in the data centre space. We invested in Neysa, which is a neo cloud.Blackstone has had a tremendous run in India–you have $50 billion deployed here. What has helped you succeed? Well, it starts with the people. Amit Dixit, who runs our private equity business, Tuhin Parikh, who runs our real estate business, have been with us now for several decades. They’ve really been builders of businesses. They’ve started with things that are very small or started from scratch. They’ve decided to start with something small, add capacity to it, maybe do additional acquisitions, put in place world-class management teams, ultimately take these businesses public. We’ve taken 14 companies public in India, five of the six REITs. We helped create the REIT rules here, working with this government that’s done such a good job.What can you tell us about Blackstone’s road map in terms of investments? It will definitely be playing this rising middle class. People are going to travel more. They’re going to consume more financial services. Healthcare certainly is going to be high on their list. We’re developing housing. We’ve invested in financial institutions who finance housing. All the things that happen as you move from a country with a very low GDP per capita, and many of those people move up, they’re going to want to consume. Providing those services is really important. I think this AI build-out is critically important. I think energy, which is an area India’s made a lot of progress in. The Prime Minister talked about progress in the solar space. I think renewables are very exciting. The digital infrastructure, the data centres and compute are really important.You have $50 billion invested in India. How much would you like that figure to be?In five years, we’d love that number to be $100 billion. Now we’ve got to find great businesses. It could be in private equity, could be in real estate. We're going to be expanding here in infrastructure. We're looking to expand in credit. I think growth equity is an opportunity. I think there's more we can do in more sectors. As the Indian market grows, it really works well for our business. People in India don’t fully appreciate just how strong your capital markets have become. The stock market’s up five and a half times in the last 20 years. It is probably, after the US, the easiest place to list a company, and that is very good for foreign capital because when you think about investing money, and in particular our drawdown funds, we’ve got to send the capital back to our investors. So the fact that India has a robust public market is very helpful. It’s another reason we have a lot of confidence here. In August, we sold more than a billion dollars of stock in a company, Knowledge Realty. To do a billion-dollar secondary speaks of the scale of this market, that there is real liquidity, and that is definitely helping our investors. It’s helping investments here. And so even as the stock market has pulled back here, the liquidity has really been maintained. And again, I think the government is continuing to make the market easier to access, yes, for foreign investors.There is some concern that we’re seeing in terms of public markets in India. In 2026 alone, foreign portfolio investors have pulled out $37 billion... Public market investors can be fickle. There was a simple narrative last year, which is that India is an importer of a lot of energy, and energy costs are going up, and that made investors cautious. India has exposure to IT services—AI’s coming. Simple narratives get established and then as money comes out, the market obviously has underperformed. But the public market can fall back into love again too. If the earnings growth, which I think is expected this quarter to be mid-teens, continues, the revenue and earnings growth, then you’ll see global investors come back.When you market your own funds and products to your LPs, are you facing any pushback? What is the sentiment about India like among global investors? The sentiment is still fairly positive. Global investors recognise there aren’t that many global firms who have boots on the ground who are capable of executing at scale. They want exposure to private market assets in India, but there’s a relatively small number of firms who can access it. The currency depreciation has been the other headwind for global investors. That’s probably the biggest question we get about India. But I think there’s increasingly more and more belief that this story has real legs.You’re significantly invested in software services, data centres, AI infrastructure, healthcare. Any other sectors or themes that have caught your fancy? Well, definitely travel, the hotel business. We invested in a visa processing business, VFS. We think foreign travelers are going to come to India more and more, particularly as the infrastructure improves. The airports here- –most people who come to India for the first time are shocked when they see the first-class nature of the airports now. As the roadways get better, travel is an area. Definitely energy in every form that you can come by. And, manufacturing will continue to be important.Financial services certainly, because you have an economy where you’re just starting to get people into markets. More and more people, as they get wealth, are going to look to invest, save, buy a house.You’ve taken a minority position in Federal Bank. We’ve been hearing murmurs about other Blackstone deals in the financial services space. Is that an area you’re beginning to get excited about? For sure. We’ve had success with Aadhar in the home lending business, ASK in the wealth management business. I just think that’s a natural part when you get this sort of increasing GDP, increasing wealth. Financial services are something that people begin to access. The banking system, the stock market, there- ’ll be all sorts of things. The insurance industry offers opportunities as well.Between Blackstone, KKR, Bain, Brookfield and EQT, some $50 billion have been raised for Asia funds. Typically, a third of that tends to come to India. Are there enough quality companies and scale opportunities to absorb so much capital? The Indian economy is now over $4 trillion. The stock market is over $5 trillion. When you think about those as the denominator, as the potential pool of investable assets, this is a place that can absorb a fair amount of capital, certainly relative to the amount of money raised in other parts of the world. I would say we are constantly pushing our teams to find new things here, but we haven’t found that we’ve had to compromise the bar.Globally, private credit has had a few challenges over the last few years. Are you seeing challenges ease up? What’s interesting is there was all this noise around private credit, and yet we haven’t seen what these sort of town criers of private credit doom were predicting, which was mass defaults and all these issues. Had they come out and said, “You know, you were operating in an environment two or three years ago where rates were really elevated, spreads were high, and there were no losses, and returns we think are going to come down a bit,” that would’ve been a very credible criticism. Instead, you’ve got a lot of noise and it led investors to say, “Whoa, I’m concerned” and it led to redemptions. I think the reality will be different, and we’ll see that wave ebb.I think there was some moderation in returns. But these products are remarkably resilient because they’re generally lowly leveraged, and they made low loan-to-value loans themselves. You’ll continue to see private credit, both on the investment and non-investment grade side, continue to take a lot of share.You love running in New York’s Central Park. Do you plan to run in India? Yes, I do plan on running in India. When you’re traveling the world, there’s no better way to see a place than to do it on foot. Right? And so, to wake up in Delhi or Mumbai or Tokyo or Brussels or wherever you are in the world, that to me is always a nice thing to do, run along the water somewhere

"Keeping investors uncertain about the level policymakers may be trying to justify can help prevent markets from anticipating official interventions.""My view is a practitioner has the ability of speaking what is going to be effective in markets," he said, adding that policymakers should avoid giving markets a specific level to speculate on.The recent pressure on the rupee was driven more by portfolio investment outflows than by the current account. The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) over the weekend announced a slew of measures to stem rupee fall.In a latest move, the central bank announced the creation of a special window for oil marketing companies, which is set to take the dollar demand away from the spot market and tightened rules governing forex derivatives trades to curb speculative bets against the rupee.Following the RBI measures, the Indian rupee strengthened for the third straight session on Tuesday and appreciated 40 paise to close at 95.38 (provisional) against the US dollar.(With inputs from agencies)

articles.summary: In the September quarter, Puravankara Ltd reported a remarkable surge in sales bookings, hitting Rs 2,136 crore, a jump from Rs 1,322 crore a year earlier. With the sales area expanding by 22 percent to 1.83 million square feet, the company also successfully delivered 977 homes, which amount to 0.97 million square feet. Puravankara's strategic focus remains on sustaining growth while optimizing pricing and capital management.

articles.title: Sebi extends easier IPO rules till March 2027, bankers lobby says
articles.summary: The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) on Tuesday extended a temporary relaxation that allows companies planning to launch initial public offerings (IPOs) to revise the size of their fresh issues without filing fresh draft documents, providing greater flexibility to issuers navigating volatile market conditions.

articles.title: Hyundai Motor Group to plug $15.5 billion in India's automotive sector
articles.summary: Hyundai Motor Group intends to invest $15.5 billion in India between 2026 and 2032. This investment aims to position India as a key market for the company's growth and expansion. The discussions about this initiative occurred during a meeting with Prime Minister Narendra Modi Ji. Executive Chair Euisun Chung emphasized the importance of India for next-generation automotive innovation.

articles.title: Hyundai replicating India learnings across global markets: CEO Jose Muñoz
articles.summary: Hyundai Motor CEO Jose Muñoz says the company's India operations offer a blueprint for global markets, with long-term investments, localisation and electrification driving growth

articles.title: IT stocks post best day in 17 months; markets log biggest gain in 4 months
articles.summary: Nifty IT surged 5.22 per cent, its biggest gain since May 2025, as the Sensex and Nifty rose over 1.5 per cent amid a selloff in Asian chip stocks and strong HCL Tech results

articles.title: CSM Tech wins $174,000 deal to digitise Mozambique's Beira trade corridor
articles.summary: The company will develop a digital observatory for Mozambique's Beira Corridor to monitor cargo movement, transport delays and trade bottlenecks across Southern Africa
